name: Mohenjo-daro
info: Mohenjo-daro was a planned city of the Indus Valley Civilisation on the lower Indus in what is now Sindh, Pakistan, built around 2500 BCE, abandoned by about 1700 BCE and now an archaeological site.

facts.founded: Built around 2500 BCE within the Indus Valley Civilisation; the founders are not known.
facts.where: Off the right (west) bank of the lower Indus river, on a Pleistocene ridge in the flood plain, in Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan, about 28 kilometres from the town of Larkana.
facts.known: One of the largest settlements of the Indus Valley Civilisation; a planned grid layout; the Citadel and the Lower City; the Great Bath; more than 700 wells and covered drains; the Priest-King, the Dancing Girl and the Pashupati seal; the undeciphered Indus script
facts.today: An archaeological site in Sindh, Pakistan, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

t: Mohenjo-daro was built around 2500 BCE as a city with a planned layout on a grid, and it was one of the largest settlements of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with an estimated population of at least 40,000.
It had more than 700 wells, covered drains along its main streets and a large public bath, but no evidence shows that priests or monarchs ruled it, and its original name is unknown.
It was abandoned by about 1700 BCE, remained undocumented for around 3,700 years, and was identified by R. D. Banerji in 1919 and 1920 before excavations from 1924 revealed its plan.
dyk: Excavations have found more than 700 wells at Mohenjo-daro, about one well for every three houses, a number that is unheard of when compared with Egypt or Mesopotamia at the time.
ev: Mohenjo-daro is built on the Indus plain as one of the large cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation
The Indus civilisation goes into sudden decline and Mohenjo-daro is abandoned
R. D. Banerji visits the site, finds a flint scraper and is convinced of its antiquity
Large-scale excavations begin under Kashinath Dikshit, followed by John Marshall in 1925
The bronze statuette known as the Dancing Girl is found, and the soapstone Priest-King follows in 1927
The last major excavations, led by George Dales, end and further excavation is banned because of weathering damage
UNESCO designates the site a World Heritage Site and an agreement to fund restoration is made

sections.origins:
Mohenjo-daro stands off the right (west) bank of the lower Indus river in Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan, about 28 kilometres from the town of Larkana. It lies on a Pleistocene ridge in the flood plain of the Indus. The city was built around 2500 BCE within the Indus Valley Civilisation, also called the Harappan Civilisation, which developed around 3000 BCE from the prehistoric Indus culture. At its height that civilisation spanned much of what is now Pakistan and North India, reaching west to the Iranian border, south to Gujarat and north to an outpost in Bactria, with major urban centres at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi.

The city's original name is unknown. From his analysis of a seal found there, Iravatham Mahadevan speculated that the ancient name could have been Kukkuṭārma, "the city of the cockerel". Mohenjo-daro is the modern name, interpreted in Sindhi as "Mound of the Dead". The site was built in a relatively short period, and the water supply system and the wells were among its first planned constructions. Its layout was planned, with rectilinear buildings arranged on a grid, and most were built of fired and mortared brick.
sections.growth:
Mohenjo-daro was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and the covered area is estimated at 300 hectares. Its population is estimated at at least 40,000; the Oxford Handbook of Cities in World History offers a "weak" estimate of a peak population of around 40,000. The city prospered for several centuries. Its size, and its provision of public buildings and facilities, suggest a high level of social organisation.

The city was divided into two parts, the Citadel and the Lower City. The Citadel, a mud-brick mound around 12 metres high, supported public baths, a large residential structure designed to house about 5,000 citizens and two large assembly halls. Some buildings combined fired brick with sun-dried mud-brick and wooden superstructures, and some had two storeys.

Excavation has recovered copper and stone tools, carved seals, balance-scales and weights, gold and jasper jewellery, and bronze and copper figurines and bowls made by the lost wax technique. Furnaces on the site were used for copperworking and melting metals rather than smelting. A section in the north-eastern part of the site seems to have been dedicated to shell-working. Copper tablets carry examples of the Indus script, which has not been deciphered.
sections.rulers:
Nothing is known of the names of Mohenjo-daro's rulers. There is no evidence that priests or monarchs ruled the city, although archaeologists gave the name "Priest-King" to a seated soapstone figure found in 1927 in a building with unusually ornamental brickwork and a wall-niche. The figure is 17.5 centimetres tall and shows a neatly bearded man with pierced earlobes, a fillet around his head, an armband and a cloak with trefoil and circle motifs.

The city's size and public buildings are taken to point to a high level of social organisation, and the combination of potentially religious and administrative buildings frames Mohenjo-daro as a developed urban city. Scholars have thought the so-called College Hall a priestly residence, and a small private structure with eight bathrooms north of the Great Bath is believed to have been reserved for priests who lived on the level above.

From the fortifications and from the structure of other major Indus cities such as Harappa, scholars have postulated that Mohenjo-daro was an administrative centre. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro share a similar layout and were generally not as heavily fortified as other Indus sites. The identical city layouts of all Indus sites show that there was some kind of political or administrative centrality, but its extent and functioning remain unclear.
sections.life:
Most houses had inner courtyards, with doors that opened onto side lanes. Individual households or groups of households drew water from smaller wells, and a large central well, with a doorway onto the main street, served the general public. Covered drains lined the major streets and most likely carried waste towards the Indus. Some houses, presumably those of more prestigious inhabitants, had rooms set aside for bathing, and one building had an underground furnace, possibly for heated bathing.

Near the Citadel stood a large public bath, the "Great Bath", where steps led from a colonnaded courtyard down to a brick pool lined with bitumen, 12 metres long, 7 metres wide and 2.4 metres deep; it may have been used for religious purification. Mortimer Wheeler identified a nearby building as a "Great Granary", but Jonathan Mark Kenoyer noted the complete lack of evidence for grain there and argued that it might better be called a "Great Hall" of uncertain function.

Ivory rulers were divided into units of about 34 millimetres with decimal subdivisions, and ancient bricks in the region have dimensions that correspond to these units. Terracotta figurines of women were found, some showing domestic activities and toys, others pregnancy, believed to be offerings for fertility. A seal shows a seated figure among animals, taken by some scholars as a yogi and by others as a "proto-Shiva". Cock-fighting may have had ritual and religious significance.
sections.crises:
The city was repeatedly threatened by flooding. Large platforms, perhaps intended as defence against floods, were raised during periods of reconstruction to lift the buildings. According to a theory first advanced by Wheeler, the city could have been flooded and silted over perhaps six times and rebuilt each time in the same place. Some archaeologists believed that the site was abandoned after a final flood engulfed it in mud.

Gregory Possehl was the first to theorise that the floods were caused by overuse and expansion upon the land, and that a mud flood was not the reason the site was abandoned. He proposed constant minor floods through the year, together with land worn out by crops, pastures and the resources used for bricks and pottery.

The Indus civilisation went into sudden decline around 1700 BCE, and Mohenjo-daro was abandoned by that time, along with other large cities of the civilisation. Archaeologists have identified the foundations of eroded mud-brick walls that once surrounded the city, guard towers to the west of the main settlement and defensive fortifications to the south. The ruins then remained undocumented for around 3,700 years. A Buddhist stupa of 150 to 500 CE stood on the mound.
sections.legacy:
R. D. Banerji of the Archaeological Survey of India visited the site in 1919 and 1920, looking for the Buddhist stupa known to be there, and a flint scraper convinced him of its antiquity. Large-scale excavations followed under Kashinath Dikshit in 1924 and 1925 and John Marshall in 1925 and 1926, then in the 1930s, in 1945 under Mortimer Wheeler and in 1964 and 1965 under George Dales. After 1965 excavation was banned because of weathering damage to the exposed structures. Core drilling in 2015 showed that the site is larger than the unearthed area.

The finds were first deposited in the Lahore Museum and later moved to New Delhi. Before the Partition of India about 12,000 objects, mostly sherds of pottery, were split equally between India and Pakistan. Pakistan received the Priest-King, India the Dancing Girl and the Pashupati seal, and a small group of artefacts went to the British Museum in 1939.

The site was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980, the first in South Asia, and it is threatened by groundwater salinity and improper restoration. In 2012 Pakistani archaeologists warned that without better conservation it could disappear by 2030.

summary: Mohenjo-daro was built around 2500 BCE on the lower Indus as one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with a planned grid, a Citadel, wells and drains. It was abandoned by about 1700 BCE and is now an archaeological site in Sindh, Pakistan.
references: Jane McIntosh, The Ancient Indus Valley: New Perspectives (ABC-CLIO, 2008)
notes: Only the city's own article was available; there is no History of Mohenjo-daro article.
START/END: the article says 'built c. 2500 BCE' and 'by c. 1700 BCE had been abandoned'; both circa. The Indus civilisation 'developed c. 3000 BC' (the article's own BC, rendered BCE).
POPULATION: 'estimated population of at least 40,000' in the lead; the Oxford Handbook gives a 'weak' estimate of a peak around 40,000. Both kept, not merged.

RULERS: the article names no ruler. It says there is no evidence priests or monarchs ruled; the Priest-King name is the archaeologists'. The 'priests' readings of the College Hall and the eight-bathroom building are the article's 'thought to' and 'it is believed'. 'No known rulers' was written as a plain statement of what the article's silence and 'no evidence' allow; the editor should read this paragraph first.

FLOODING: Wheeler's six floods are 'perhaps six times'; Possehl's theory attributed as such. The article says 'some archaeologists believed' a final flood abandoned the site. Decline 'c. 1700 BCE' is called 'sudden' in the article's Historical context.
The article says the city 'was abandoned' c. 1700 BCE but the stupa of 150-500 CE stood on the site; I wrote only that a stupa 'stood on the mound', which the article implies ('known to be there').

'Ivory rulers' date: the article says circa 1500 BC for Indus rulers in general and the Mohenjo-daro ruler; that contradicts the city's abandonment c. 1700 BCE, so the date was left out. The ruler's unit is given as 34 mm.
The Dancing Girl's age (about 4,000 years), the necklace (held in a private collection, 4,500 years) and Wheeler's quotation were left out for space or doubt.

Population-related claim 'one well for every three houses' and 'unheard of' compared with Egypt and Mesopotamia are the article's; the article's claim that wells served in case of siege and its claim that the circular brick well was an Indus invention were left out as speculative.
Left out: the 2014 Sindh Festival, climate, the Mother Goddess idol detail beyond the figurines, funding figures, pottery braziers, the Etymology claim about domesticated chicken.
The article's phrase 'Mohenjo-daro was the most advanced city of its time' was left out as a ranking.
